newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM faces first test, farm blockade grows.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM faces first test, farm blockade grows.

text.p: Defiant Greek farmers erected more barricades on national road and rail links on Tuesday, causing transport chaos for a sixth day and brushing off warnings they were inflicting heavy damage on the economy.
Queues of trapped international and domestic lorries grew at more than 25 blockades, which have wreaked havoc on major roads around the country.
"We've been here for three days with no food, no water, no toilets," an international driver told television reporters at the western port of Patras.
He was carrying a cargo from Germany to the NATO base on the island of Crete. He had crossed from Italy before being trapped by the farmers.
Hundreds of trucks could be seen stretching along highways while others tried to inch their way along narrow country lanes to skirt the barricades.

The protest, backed by a motley army of some 6,000 tractors, is pressing demands for lower fuel prices, lower Value Added Tax (VAT) on equipment, higher farm subsides and rescheduling some $1.3 billion in debts with state banks.
A similar protest in 1995 lasted 10 days, sent food prices soaring and cost the economy tens of millions of dollars but the farmers seemed in a festive mood and unconcerned about economic damage.
"We're farmers. We work the fields. That's our job. Farmers can't go to Brussels to protest for their rights. That's the goverment's job," Dimitris Paskos told Reuters Television.
Bonfires of tyres lit up the night. Despite bitter cold and rain, farmers have set up sprawling motorway camps with chairs, tables and plastic tent shelters.
Tractors line the roadsides five deep and many have tied on Christmas trees to symbolise the farmers' boast that they are prepared to stay put through the coming holidays.
It is the first challenge to the economic policies of Prime Minister Costas Simitis since his socialist party won elections in September.

Simitis's priority is meeting the European Union's strict targets for economic and monetary union. He has ignored calls by the farmers for a direct meeting and let his senior officials do the talking.

"Intransigence does not benefit the farmers' problems or the country. The government is not prepared to negotiate the course of the country. Everyone must understand that the situation must not and cannot continue," said spokesman Yannis Nikolaou.
The farmers turned down government compromise proposals on Monday, saying they fell miserably short of their demands.
Asked if police would force open the roads, Nikolaou said: "We have not reached the point to be discussing such an option."
The blockade coincides with a string of strikes planned by other groups to protest against Simitis's 1997 austerity budget which was submitted to parliament last week.
"A course is set for the country towards EU convergence. The government cannot, and is not allowed to turn back from this course however just the demands," Nikolaou said.
